node.label: Donald Creighton
node.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
node.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Creighton (1902–1979); The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1760–1850 (1937; reissued as The Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1956); Dominion of the North: A History of Canada (1944); John A. Macdonald: The Young Politician (1952) and The Old Chieftain (1955); Presidential Address, Canadian Historical Association (1957); Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (1957); “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” (1969); Canada’s First Century, 1867–1967 (1970). Readings: Heaton (1938); Brunet (1953); Frégault (1955); Woodcock (1979); Ouellet (1984); Davis (1985); Salmon (1997); Buckner (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only).

proposed_edges.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The laurentian strand names Creighton (with Innis) and cites the 1937 book, the Macdonald biography and Salmon; the evidence fits it. The liberal_conservative_nationalists strand (Buckner's grouping) and analysing_tradition (Berger, Miville) also hold his name, but they record readings of him, not his contribution.

proposed_edges.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
proposed_edges.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Person entries carry no strands. The matching group strand is cdn_national_tradition/laurentian, which names both men; edge_897 (harold_a_innis → cdn_national_tradition) targets the staples strand and stays.
proposed_edges.include_note: Kept because Creighton's own texts use the staple framework and name Innis's books, and readers from 1979 to 1997 describe the lineage. Wording follows his 1969 qualification. Reviewers may prefer to leave the lineage to the laurentian strand alone (both names already sit there); if so, set include false.

proposed_edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The progressive strand lists Turner and gives 'Turner’s frontier essay' among its works; Creighton attacks that thesis. multiple_hypotheses is Turner's later methodological address, which Creighton does not discuss.
proposed_edges.include_note: A critique in his own words of a position the atlas entry holds (Turner's frontier thesis). The progressive entry is a US field; edge_798 (progressive — cdn_national_tradition, comparison) stays, since it compares consensus history, not the frontier thesis.

proposed_edges.relationship: The 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle', as Canadian party intellectuals applied it in the 1930s, rejected as alien to Canadian experience (1957)
proposed_edges.map_label: Against the class-struggle reading of Canada, 1957
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 presidential address (read in full): the 'Marxian economic interpretation of history' was 'a doctrine which was alien to their experience and unremunerative for their purposes' (p. 6); the League for Social Reconstruction, 'the "brains trust" of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation', insisted that 'the real work of the Fathers of Confederation had been to establish an economic empire for the entrepreneurs of Montreal' (pp. 6–7); 'Canadian history was a sadly imperfect vehicle for the exemplification of the Marxian verities' (p. 7). He exempts Innis, who 'refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). The target is a Canadian application, named only through the LSR; no Marx text or Marxist historian on the karl roster is discussed.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No karl strand concerns Canadian or 1930s party applications of the class-struggle doctrine.
proposed_edges.include_note: Excluded by the drafter: the passage criticises the LSR's use of Marxism in Canada, not a position any karl strand or roster member states, so an arrow to karl would overstate its object. Recorded for the editor; the frontier edge (3) carries the 1957 critique.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed as a critique. In 1969 he wrote that Confederation was 'a political agreement among several provinces, not ... a cultural compact between two cultural groups' (p. 18) and that the ideas of duality, bilingualism and a special position for Quebec were 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation' (p. 25), but he names no Quebec historian: the target is public and constitutional opinion, not an atlas entry's historiographical position. Ouellet (1984, p. 227) notes that the Montreal school's account of the Conquest (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) resembled Creighton's 'décapitation sociale' scheme; Brunet's and Frégault's reviews (1953, 1955) are the Quebec critics. edge_799 (cdn_national_tradition — quebec_historiography, comparison, with Miville on Creighton and Brunet) already carries the comparison; these readings are recorded on edge 1 and in the node.

Not proposed. Woodcock (1979, p. 135) calls the Macdonald volumes 'the first important study of the most interesting political personality Canada has yet produced' and praises 'Creighton's literary artistry'; Brunet (1953) and Frégault (1955) criticise the biographer's hero-making ('un homme ne crée pas une nation', Frégault, p. 444). But Creighton himself presents the biography as the second phase of 'a trilogy on one theme' (1969, p. 16), so it is folded into edge 1; the biography entry's strands are international and none concerns national political biography.

Not proposed. Its political_biography strand (Brown, Bélanger, English) and external_relations strand are post-1970 work; Creighton has no roster row there. The Forked Road (1976), his history of 1939–57, is the work Canadian dissertations cite most (see citation_evidence), but it was not read and its reception was not checked.

Not proposed. Davis (1985, p. 97) counts him among the 'deans' of five metropolitan approaches and quotes Harrison that he was 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation'; the metropolitanism strand of cdn_national_tradition belongs to Careless (drafted separately), and edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) already records urban historians' rejection of the metropolitan thesis. Davis reports Careless saying he drew 'neither from Creighton or Innis' (p. 101), so no Creighton → Careless arrow is proposed either.
Morton has no person entry, and his texts are unread here (known through Davis 1985). edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional critique of the national frame.

edges_considered_not_proposed.pair: donald_creighton → cdn_national_tradition (critique of the Liberal 'Authorized Version')
edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: The 1957 address (pp. 4–5) attacks the 'Liberal Interpretation — or Authorized Version' of Dafoe, Skelton and the King biographers, and Woodcock (1979, p. 139) quotes his 1972 statement that the Liberal view was 'almost a complete inversion of my own'. The Liberal nationalists sit inside cdn_national_tradition (liberal_conservative_nationalists strand) beside Creighton himself, so a critique arrow would point at the entry his contribution edge also targets. Recorded in the node instead.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 14–25) from page images of the Érudit PDF, via the Internet Archive capture of 25 July 2024 (the live Érudit site returned a bot-check page); OCR checked against the page order and running heads. Quoted: the phrase 'made its first public appearance in the autumn of 1937' (he names the book The Empire of the St. Lawrence, its 1956 title); regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'; the book as 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis' called a simple generalization that 'happen[s] to be wrong' (p. 14); subject suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy'; the Chateau Clique merchants and 'Montreal's staple trades' (p. 15); 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence'; 'The protagonist of the Empire of the St. Lawrence was the River itself'; Macdonald as 'the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase' and 'a trilogy on one theme'; 'This Laurentian theme ...' and 'a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (p. 16); 'the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); Confederation 'not of a cultural compact between two cultural groups' (p. 18); the First World War as 'the great divide' (p. 19); Mackenzie King 'not so much a Canadian citizen as a citizen of North America' (p. 21); 'Canada now stands alone' and 'American economic and military imperialism' (p. 22); 'ethnic and cultural values' (p. 24); duality, bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation' (p. 25).

new_sources.scope_note: The author's own retrospect on the Laurentian theme (1969) and his account of its 'decline and fall'; a later statement, not evidence of the 1937 text.

Cet axe vital est à la fois transocéanique et transcontinental' (p. 529). It is the reviewer's summary of Creighton's portrait, not Innis's own words.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review: Creighton's portrait of Innis in Laurentian terms, as reported.

verification.note: Read in full (journal PDF on UBC's OJS; issue 83, pp. 131–141). A literary critic's essay, not a historian's. Quoted: Creighton 'glorifying the transcontinental conception of the original Dominion-builders', and his Maclean's article 'No More Concessions' (27 June 1977) (p. 133); 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis ... with Innis's encouragement' (p. 134); the Macdonald volumes 'the first important study of the most interesting political personality Canada has yet produced' (p. 135); 'the dominant vision is spatial even more than temporal' (p. 137); Creighton's 1972 introduction to Towards the Discovery of Canada calling the Liberal view 'almost a complete inversion of my own' (p. 139; quoted by Woodcock, not read); 'a major distortion in Creighton's view of Canadian history' and 'the fallacy that the Fathers of Confederation did not intend to create a genuine federalism' (p. 140).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period critical essay pairing Creighton and Groulx as national myth-makers.

verification.note: Pp. 225–229 read (Érudit PDF, Internet Archive capture of 15 August 2022, text layer); the rest unread. Quoted: Creighton, 'partant de la théorie des staples pour établir les bases économiques du développement de la nation canadienne', held that New France's economy rested on the fur trade and was led by a bourgeoisie (p. 226, n. 13 citing the 1937 and 1944 books); 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; his post-Conquest French Canada 'une société semi-féodale décadente devenue hostile aux impératifs économiques'; Ouellet asks whether the later scheme of Séguin, Frégault and Brunet is 'bien différent' (p. 227).

new_sources.scope_note: A Quebec historiographical survey placing Creighton's Conquest argument before the Montreal school's.

cdng_davis_1985.note: Read in full for the 1.135 Creighton entry (Érudit PDF via the Internet Archive capture of 26 September 2024; UHR 14:2, October 1985, pp. 95–113). Careless's 1954 article 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (p. 95); Harrison (1981, p. 25) quoted: Creighton 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1980 reprint, p. 107) quoted: Creighton emphasized 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played'; Morton ('Canada's History and Historians', reprint pp. 34–35) quoted: the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (pp. 97–98); Careless said he drew 'neither from Creighton or Innis' but from medieval social history and N. S. B. Gras, and melded Gras with 'the Laurentian School, then regnant' (p. 101). Morton's texts themselves are unread.
